sentences.text: Researchers analyzed cognitive test scores and gut bacteria samples from 867 older adults and compared these data with a mouse model where animals learned locations in a water maze. Mice receiving gut bacteria from humans with faster thinking skills showed better memory and more brain cells than those receiving bacteria from slower thinkers. By combining data from people and mice, the study proposes that changes in bacterial metabolism drive improvements in brain function.

Better cognitive performance in both people and mice was linked to specific chemical pathways involving arginine, proline, and pterins. Mice given bacteria from high-performing humans showed brain changes related to dopamine, including more dopamine receptors and less reuptake of the chemical. The authors suggest that gut bacteria may influence thinking speed and memory specifically in older people.
